taxonomy.subtopic: Reactivation of latent tissue cysts in advanced HIV

questions.stem_html:
A 41-year-old man with untreated HIV infection presents with headache, fever, confusion, and left-arm weakness. His CD4 count is 38/mm3. MRI shows several ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia with surrounding edema. Toxoplasma IgG is positive. He improves after pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin.

Which process most likely produced these brain lesions?

options.text_html: Primary infection of erythrocytes followed by sequestration in cerebral capillaries
Progressive multifocal infection of oligodendrocytes by JC virus
Reactivation of latent bradyzoite-containing tissue cysts after loss of cell-mediated immune control
Hematogenous spread of encapsulated yeast from the lungs
Integration of protozoal DNA into CD4-positive lymphocytes

questions.explanation_html: Toxoplasma establishes persistent bradyzoite cysts in neural and muscle tissue. Profound T-cell deficiency permits conversion to replicating tachyzoites, causing necrotizing encephalitis. Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in advanced HIV with positive prior-exposure IgG are most consistent with reactivation of latent tissue cysts.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Erythrocyte infection and sequestration describe falciparum malaria, not toxoplasmosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: JC virus causes nonenhancing white-matter lesions and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Cryptococcus commonly causes meningitis rather than multiple basal-ganglia abscess-like lesions.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Toxoplasma does not cause disease through genomic integration into lymphocytes.

questions.educational_objective: Distinguish cerebral toxoplasmosis from other HIV-associated neurologic diseases by recognizing reactivation, multiple ring-enhancing basal-ganglia lesions, and severe CD4 depletion.
